g10-geography-ug6-t1.overview: Today over 7 billion people live on the planet and the number keeps rising, putting huge pressure on the natural environment. This lesson defines population change and growth and traces the size, share and growth rate of every continent, with special attention to sub-Saharan Africa.
objectives: Define population change and population growth and distinguish between them
Identify the factors that increase and decrease the number of individuals in a population
Describe Africa's population stagnation between 1500 and 1900 and account for its causes
Compare the continents by population size, share and growth rate in 2021
Explain why understanding population trends matters for development planning and the 2030 Agenda
g10-geography-ug6-t1.simple: Population change is the difference in the size of a population from the beginning to the end of a period. Population growth is the increase in the number of individuals in a population. Fertility (birth) and immigration (in-migration) raise the number of individuals, while mortality (death) and emigration (out-migration) lower it. Understanding these changes at local, national, regional and global scales is vital for development planning, including the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Between 1500 and 1900 Africa's population almost stagnated, rising only from 80 million to 100 million, because of slave trade, colonization and deadly diseases. In the twentieth century the developing world exploded demographically, and sub-Saharan Africa grew fastest. Asia and Africa are the only continents with more than one billion people.
g10-geography-ug6-t1.detailed:
Population change and population growth. Population change is the difference in the size of the population from the beginning to the end of a certain period. The change also alters the composition of the population through birth and death rates, sex ratios, life expectancies and migration rates. Population growth is the increase in the number of individuals in a population. Two factors increase the number of individuals: fertility (birth) and immigration (in-migration). On the other hand, mortality (death) and emigration (out-migration) decrease it. Understanding these changes at different spatial scales - local, national, regional and global - is very important for development planning.

Population change and the 2030 Agenda. Anticipating demographic change is crucial for development goals such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, which puts people at the center of sustainable development. Population trends over past decades show progress toward several Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): reduced mortality, particularly among children, and increased access to sexual and reproductive health care through population policies and family planning programs. The challenges differ by region. Countries with rapid growth - most of them in sub-Saharan Africa - must provide schooling and health care to growing numbers of children and prepare education and employment for more youth. Countries where growth has slowed or ceased must prepare health care for an increasing proportion of older persons.

The stagnation of Africa's population, 1500-1900. Slave trade, colonization and the spread of deadly diseases caused population stagnation in sub-Saharan Africa. Between 1500 and 1900 Africa's population grew by only 20 million people, from 80 million in 1500 A.D. to 100 million in 1900 A.D. During the same period the populations of other regions, such as Asia, South America and North America, increased three to fivefold.

The demographic explosion of the developing world. The twentieth century witnessed the demographic explosion of the developing world. Between 1900 and 1980 all developing regions, including sub-Saharan Africa, experienced high population growth. The growth rate of sub-Saharan Africa stood at 2.8 percent per year on average. Between 1980 and 2015 the three major sub-regions - Eastern Africa at 2.9 percent, Central Africa at 3.0 percent and Western Africa at 2.7 percent per year on average - together represented about 93.5 percent of the continent's population in 2015. The Southern sub-region grew more slowly, at 1.8 percent per year. By mid-2015 the sub-Saharan Africa population was estimated at 962 million, about ten times its 1900 level. Today the continent has more than 1.3 billion people and is increasing at an annual rate of 2.45 percent.

The continents compared. Asia is the most populous continent, with 4.68 billion people, or 59.5 percent of the world population as of 2021. Africa is second with around 1.37 billion people, or 17.2 percent. Only these two continents have crossed the one-billion milestone, and together they share about 77 percent of the global population. Europe has about 748 million people (9.59 percent), North America about 597 million (7.60 percent), and South America, the second least populated continent, about 434 million (5.53 percent). Oceania, with 43 million people (0.55 percent), is the smallest continent. The world population stood at about 7.87 billion in 2021, having increased by about 80.2 million during that year alone.

Why the world population grew so fast. The high growth of the past centuries is largely the result of advances in modern medicines and improvements in living standards. These reduced infant, child and maternal mortality and increased life expectancy, which in turn raised the world population.

keyTerms.def: The difference in the size of the population from the beginning to the end of a certain period, which also changes the population's composition.
The increase in the number of individuals in a population.
Birth; one of the two factors that increase the number of individuals in a population.
Death; one of the two factors that decrease the number of individuals in a population.
In-migration; arrival of people into a population, which increases its size.
Out-migration; departure of people from a population, which decreases its size.
The very rapid population growth of the developing world during the twentieth century.
The average number of years a person is expected to live; it rose as modern medicines and better living standards reduced mortality.

workedExamples.problem: Using the doubling time approach from Unit 4, how many years will it take Africa's population to double if it grows at 2.45 percent per year?
workedExamples.given: Africa's annual population growth rate in 2021 was 2.45 percent.
workedExamples.formula: Doubling time (years) = 70 / annual growth rate in percent
workedExamples.answer: At 2.45 percent growth, Africa's population doubles in about 29 years.

workedExamples.problem: How long would Europe's population take to double at its 2021 growth rate of 0.01 percent per year?
workedExamples.given: Europe's annual population growth rate in 2021 was 0.01 percent.
workedExamples.formula: Doubling time (years) = 70 / annual growth rate in percent
workedExamples.answer: About 7,000 years - Europe's population is growing so slowly that it is nearly stationary.

workedExamples.problem: The world population was 7,794,798,729 in 2020 and 7,874,965,732 in 2021. Calculate the net change and the annual growth rate.
workedExamples.formula: Population change = later population - earlier population; growth rate = (net change / earlier population) x 100
workedExamples.calculation: Net change = 80,167,003 people; rate = 80,167,003 / 7,794,798,729 x 100 = about 1.03 percent.
workedExamples.answer: The world added about 80.2 million people in one year, a growth rate of about 1.03 percent.

commonMistakes: Using 'population change' and 'population growth' as if they mean the same thing.
Saying emigration increases a population; out-migration decreases it while immigration increases it.
Attributing Africa's 1500-1900 stagnation to climate or disease alone, forgetting slave trade and colonization.
Assuming all continents grow at similar rates; Europe grew 0.01 percent in 2021 while Africa grew 2.45 percent.
Confusing a continent's share of world population with its actual size; Oceania has the smallest share, 0.55 percent.
Believing rapid growth comes only from more births, when lower infant, child and maternal mortality and longer life expectancy are the main causes.
applications: Use the doubling time rule with your district's annual growth rate to estimate when schools and clinics must be expanded.
Explain why a country like fast-growing ones in sub-Saharan Africa must invest in youth education and employment before the population doubles.
Use the age and size of a population to plan services, since policymakers must know how many people live in an area, where they are, and how old they are.
Interpret Table 6.1 to argue why development plans differ between Africa, which grew 2.45 percent in 2021, and Europe, which grew 0.01 percent.
Connect family planning and reproductive health programs to the SDGs by showing how they reduced child mortality in many countries.
Anticipate how rapid population growth in Africa pressures water, land and food supplies, which the rest of this unit addresses.
g10-geography-ug6-t1.summary: Population change is the difference in a population's size from the beginning to the end of a period, while population growth is the increase in the number of individuals, driven by births and immigration and reduced by deaths and emigration. After stagnating between 1500 and 1900 because of slave trade, colonization and deadly diseases, Africa's population grew explosively in the twentieth century and now exceeds 1.3 billion, growing at 2.45 percent per year. Reading these trends helps countries plan schooling, health care and development in line with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

g10-geography-ug6-t2.overview: Human beings and the environment affect each other in a two-way relationship: people depend on nature, modify it and adapt to its changes. This lesson explains the two leading theories about the human role and the three types of human-environment interaction.
objectives: Define environment as a multidimensional system that supports life
Explain why the human-environment relationship is two-way or reciprocal
Distinguish environmental determinism from environmental possibilism
Describe how humans depend on and modify the environment, positively and negatively
Classify adaptation responses into grey, green and soft measures and identify autonomous and planned adaptation
g10-geography-ug6-t2.simple: Environment means the surroundings or conditions in which persons, animals or plants live. Humans interact with it to satisfy their increasing needs, and the relationship is two-way: people change the environment and the environment changes people. Two theories explain the human role. Environmental determinism, popular among Europeans in the nineteenth century, says the physical environment dictates culture and controls human activities; it was rejected in the 1950s. Environmental possibilism says people can choose from many possibilities despite environmental limits, so environmental influence declines with modernization. Interaction takes three forms: dependence (obtaining food, water, shelter and clothing), modification (cutting forests, building dams, drilling for oil) and adaptation (adjusting to change to improve chances of survival), through technological, ecosystem-based or behavioral responses.
g10-geography-ug6-t2.detailed:
What the environment is. Environment is defined as the surroundings or conditions in which persons, animals or plants live or operate. It refers to all of the external factors affecting an organism. It is therefore a multidimensional system of complex relationships in a continuing state of change, not a fixed backdrop.

Why humans interact with the environment, and how. The objective of human interaction with the environment is to satisfy human beings' increasing needs. The relationship runs in a two-way or reciprocal direction: people and the environment affect each other. Humans cannot survive without some form of interaction with the environment, and interaction is seen in how people depend on, modify and adapt to the environment - the three types of human-environment interaction.

Two theories about the human role. Environmental determinism is the idea that the natural or physical environment shapes and creates cultures; in other words the environment essentially dictates culture. It asserts that economic growth and other human activities are controlled by the physical environment. This view was commonly propagated by Europeans in the 19th century, but it was rejected in the 1950s and substituted by environmental possibilism. Environmental possibilism asserts that people can adapt to diverse environmental conditions and choose from many alternatives despite the limitations the environment poses. It is the opposite of determinism, and its key insight is that the influence of the natural environment declines with increasing modernization and technological advancement.

Dependence on the environment. Every living thing depends on the environment to obtain essential resources. Humans depend on it for food, since plants grow from the soil and feed the goats, sheep and cattle that people eat; water, provided as rain, rivers, lakes and oceans and used for drinking, washing, irrigation and power generation; shelter, built from sand, stones and trees; and clothing, made from raw materials such as silk and cotton. The environment also supports economic activities directly, by providing resources and raw materials such as water, timber and minerals as inputs for goods and services, and indirectly, through ecosystem services including carbon sequestration, water purification, managing flood risks and nutrient cycling. These provisions safeguard growth and development for present and future generations.

Modification of the environment. Humans modify the environment negatively or positively to fulfill their needs. Examples include cutting down forests to increase agricultural land, constructing dams to store water for hydroelectricity and irrigation and to avoid floods, and drilling holes in the ground to extract oil. As population increases, more food and more resources are needed, so humans cause impacts such as overpopulation, pollution, burning fossil fuels and deforestation. Changes like these have triggered climate change, soil erosion, poor air quality and undrinkable water. The environment also casts negative impacts on people: natural calamities like floods, drought, wildfires, earthquakes and tsunamis can cause large-scale migration and death. Humans also have positive effects: through afforestation and conservation they improve air quality, reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide and protect endangered species.

Adaptation and adaptation responses. Adaptation is an adjustment to a new environment - or to actual or expected environmental changes such as rising temperature and flooding - so as to improve the chances of survival. It prepares people to reduce vulnerability, identify the most vulnerable people, build adaptive capacity, reduce exposure or sensitivity to impacts and ensure sustainable development. Adapting human systems takes a process: engage governmental and nongovernmental stakeholders, analyze current exposure to shocks and stresses and future impacts such as climate change, deforestation and desertification, understand vulnerability, design and implement strategies, then monitor, evaluate and share lessons. The results, called adaptation responses, fall into three broad categories: technological solutions (grey measures), which are expensive and need research and training; ecosystem-based options (green measures), low-cost nature-based solutions such as reforestation that can stop desertification and recharge groundwater in drought; and behavioral, managerial and policy approaches (soft measures), which also build resilience at low cost.

Types of adaptation, and what cannot be modified. Autonomous (spontaneous) adaptation is not a conscious response to environmental change; it is triggered by ecological changes in natural systems and by market or lifestyle changes in human systems. Planned adaptation results from a deliberate policy decision, based on the awareness that conditions have changed or are about to change and that action is required. Some conditions humans cannot modify at all, so they adapt instead: taking benefit of the natural slope of the land for irrigation, building houses on higher ground to avoid floods, wearing thin clothes in hot climates and warm clothes in cold climate.

keyTerms.def: The surroundings or conditions in which persons, animals or plants live or operate; all external factors affecting an organism.
A two-way interaction in which human beings and the environment affect each other.
The 19th-century doctrine that the physical environment shapes cultures and controls human activities; rejected in the 1950s.
The theory that people can choose from many possible responses despite environmental limits, whose influence declines with modernization.
The reliance of humans on the environment for food, water, shelter, clothing and economic inputs.
Deliberate human changing of the environment, positively or negatively, to extract and use its resources.
An adjustment to a new or changing environment, in natural or human systems, to improve the chances of survival.
Adaptation that follows a deliberate policy decision based on awareness that conditions have changed or are about to change.

workedExamples.problem: A valley prone to flooding uses three measures: concrete embankments, community reforestation of the hillside, and a public education plus land-use policy program. Classify each as a grey, green or soft measure.
workedExamples.given: Measure 1 is engineered construction; measure 2 restores an ecosystem; measure 3 changes behavior and rules.
workedExamples.formula: Grey = technological solutions; green = ecosystem-based options; soft = behavioral, managerial and policy approaches.
workedExamples.substitution: Embankments are engineered; reforestation is nature-based; education and policy alter behavior and management.
workedExamples.calculation: Each measure matches exactly one category, so classification is unambiguous.
workedExamples.answer: Embankments are grey measures, reforestation is a green measure, and education with land-use policy is a soft measure.

workedExamples.problem: Farmers quietly begin shifting their sowing dates as rains arrive later each year, while the government separately launches a program to build flood shelters after a flood-risk assessment. Which is autonomous and which is planned adaptation?
workedExamples.given: The farmers act without any policy; the government acts through a deliberate program.
workedExamples.formula: Autonomous (spontaneous) adaptation is not a conscious response to environmental change; planned adaptation is the result of a deliberate policy decision.
workedExamples.substitution: Farmers' timing shift follows ecological and market changes in human systems; the program is a conscious decision.
workedExamples.calculation: Only the government program is based on an awareness that conditions have changed and action is required.
workedExamples.answer: The farmers' shift is autonomous (spontaneous) adaptation; the government program is planned adaptation.

workedExamples.problem: A traveler notes that people irrigate fields downhill slopes, farm hot deserts, and in cold areas wear warm clothes while desert dwellers wear thin clothes. Which theory - determinism or possibilism - best explains these human choices?
workedExamples.given: People use the land's natural slope for irrigation and adjust clothing to different climates.
workedExamples.formula: Determinism claims the environment dictates culture; possibilism claims people choose among possibilities.
workedExamples.substitution: The people studied their environmental conditions and actively selected suitable practices.
workedExamples.calculation: Because humans chose workable alternatives within environmental limits, the record shows choice, not environmental control.
workedExamples.answer: Possibilism; humans adapt and choose alternatives, so environmental influence declines with modernization and technology.

workedExamples.problem: A family drinks water from a river, a city drains a wetland to build houses, and a village builds its houses on higher ground to escape floods. Classify each action as dependence, modification or adaptation.
workedExamples.given: Action 1 draws a resource; action 2 changes the land; action 3 adjusts to a hazard.
workedExamples.formula: Dependence obtains essential resources; modification alters the environment; adaptation adjusts to environmental changes.
workedExamples.substitution: Drinking river water is a direct use; draining the wetland alters it; building on higher ground reduces flood exposure.
workedExamples.calculation: Each action fits exactly one of the three types of human-environment interaction.
workedExamples.answer: Dependence (drinking the river water), modification (draining the wetland), adaptation (building on higher ground).

commonMistakes: Thinking the human-environment relationship is one-way, with humans acting on nature and nothing returning; the textbook calls it two-way or reciprocal.
Saying environmental determinism was accepted in the 1950s; it was rejected in the 1950s and replaced by possibilism.
Believing humans can modify every environmental condition; some, like the land's natural slope, can only be used through adaptation.
Calling all adaptation technological; green (ecosystem-based) and soft (behavioral, managerial and policy) measures are often cheaper.
Confusing autonomous adaptation with planned adaptation; spontaneous response is not a deliberate policy decision.
Listing modification as always harmful; afforestation and conservation are positive modifications.
Forgetting that dependence covers clothing and shelter as well as food and water.
applications: Trace the everyday breakfast you eat back to the environment: soil-grown crops, rain-fed cattle and cloth made from plants.
Ask why a house in a flood-prone valley should stand on higher ground and discuss what would happen if it ignored the slope.
Compare a costly grey project such as a large dam with low-cost green measures such as reforestation that recharges groundwater in drought.
Explain how afforestation in a deforested upland improves air quality and protects endangered species, a positive modification.
Argue with possibilism that a community can modernize its farming on a dry hillside instead of abandoning the land.
Use the reciprocal relationship to warn that polluting a river today returns undrinkable water to the same community tomorrow.
g10-geography-ug6-t2.summary: The environment is the surroundings of all living things, and the human-environment relationship is a two-way interaction: humans depend on the environment for food, water, shelter and clothing, modify it to meet their needs, and adapt to its changes to survive. Determinism, popular in the 19th century, exaggerated the environment's control over culture and was rejected in the 1950s for possibilism, which sees humans choosing among alternatives as technology advances. Adaptations are autonomous or planned, and their responses are grey, green or soft measures, but the balance between use and protection remains the key to survival.

g10-geography-ug6-t3.overview: Long before formal parks and laws, African communities conserved their forests, wildlife and water with rules, beliefs and practices passed down orally for generations. This lesson shows why indigenous knowledge matters for conservation and studies the Teso community of Kenya as a case.
objectives: Define indigenous knowledge and explain how it reached the present generation
Explain why African communities rely heavily on plant medicine
Describe the Teso community's protection of sacred sites, flora and fauna
Explain how Teso rules and beliefs conserved rivers, wells, marshes and their wildlife
Appreciate the role of indigenous knowledge in conservation and sustainable use of natural resources
g10-geography-ug6-t3.simple: Africa is endowed with rich and highly diverse biological resources used for food, housing and, above all, medicine. People rely on plant medicine because it is locally available, cheap, accepted by communities, and health centers and medical professionals are few, especially in rural areas. Indigenous knowledge is the enormous knowledge about biodiversity and its uses accumulated among African indigenous peoples and orally transferred across many generations. It has been the basis of natural resource conservation in Africa. In the Teso community of Busia County, Kenya, farming, grazing and settlement were prohibited in protected areas; remains of the dead were kept in strictly protected sites that became dense forests; and rivers, wells and their reptiles were guarded by strong rules and beliefs.
g10-geography-ug6-t3.detailed:
Biological resources and plant medicine. Africa is endowed with rich and highly diverse biological (natural) resources. Beyond the well-known uses of these resources for food and building houses, African people depend on them highly for medicinal purposes. The heavy reliance on plant medicine is attributed to four conditions: local availability, low price, acceptance by local communities, and the low number of health care centers and medical professionals, especially in rural areas. Since ancient times, plant medicine has been an important part of the health care system in Africa.

What indigenous knowledge is and why it matters. African people hold an enormous amount of knowledge about biodiversity and its uses. This indigenous knowledge has been accumulated among indigenous peoples of the continent and has been orally transferred across many generations. It has been the basis for conservation of natural resources in Africa, and it is valuable today in managing environmental degradation and in the sustainable use of natural resources.

The Teso case: protecting sacred places. A case study of the Teso community in Busia County, Kenya, by Dominics Dan Ayaa and Fuchaka Waswa (2016), shows indigenous conservation in practice. Among the Teso, activities such as farming, grazing of animals and even settlement were prohibited in protected areas. Community members believed that the spirits of long-buried relatives haunted the living family members. To respect them, there was a common practice of exhuming (digging out) the remains of the dead from graves at least ten years old. This ceremony, locally known as Ekutet or Epunyas, was carried out by a special group of elderly men and women, in the absence of children and foreigners. Special baskets transferred the recovered remains to a special central site where they were stored in strictly protected places, because spirits were believed to attack anybody disturbing the peace of the dead there.

Sacred sites become biodiverse forests. Because no human activity of any kind was carried out in such areas, the sites remained very thick forests, harboring a number of species and different organisms. Such places were considered sacred and protected from any internal or external interference. This encouraged the natural growth of vegetation that later turned out to be dense forests forming important habitats for a variety of flora and fauna.

Conserving water resources and their creatures. The Teso also recognized rivers, marshes and swamps as dwelling places of ancestors and of God's creatures (biodiversity), since various species of plants and animals thrived in them. Water courses, streams, water pans and wells, together with their associated vegetation, were conserved through rules that ensured sustainability. Reptiles such as snakes, frogs and toads that inhabited ponds, rivers and wells were protected from any harm, due to the belief that they helped maintain and sustain the lives of these important water points. Because wells and rivers were crucial sources of water for livestock and people, as well as a source of fish, strong rules and beliefs protected these sites for many generations.

The wider lesson. Nature has provided humans a sustainable and favorable environment, but humans have destroyed the balance of the natural environment by overusing resources or using them unsustainably. Although human-environment interactions are inevitable for co-existence, maintaining a suitable balance is the key to survival, and in avoiding or reducing the damage the accumulated indigenous knowledge of the African people is inevitable.

keyTerms.def: Knowledge about biodiversity and its uses accumulated among indigenous peoples and orally transferred across many generations.
The native peoples of a place whose long-settled communities hold and pass on local knowledge.
The people living in a particular area whose shared beliefs and rules govern daily use of resources.
A natural resource of living origin, such as plants and animals, used for food, housing and medicine.
The variety of plants, animals and other organisms living in an area.
The protection and careful management of natural resources so they remain usable for present and future generations.
The damage and deterioration of the environment, which indigenous knowledge helps to manage.
A place protected through beliefs and rules, where human activity is prohibited and nature regenerates freely.

workedExamples.problem: Arrange the stages of the Teso Ekutet (Epunyas) ceremony in the correct order, from the graves at least ten years old to the final conservation outcome.
workedExamples.given: Stages: remains dug out; special baskets transfer remains; elderly men and women perform the ceremony; remains stored in a strictly protected central site; site becomes dense forest.
workedExamples.formula: Sequence rule: the ceremony is performed first by the elders without children and foreigners, then the remains are moved and protected.
workedExamples.substitution: Exhume, transfer by basket, store in the protected site, prohibit all human activity there.
workedExamples.calculation: The prohibited activity is what allows vegetation to regenerate naturally into dense forest.
workedExamples.answer: Dig out remains from graves at least ten years old; elders perform the ceremony; baskets carry the remains to a special central site; human activity is banned there; thick forest with rich flora and fauna develops.

workedExamples.problem: A village far from any health center has little cash but abundant medicinal plants. Using the four conditions named in the lesson, explain why the village relies on plant medicine.
workedExamples.given: Local plants are cheap and culturally accepted; clinics and medical professionals are few in rural areas.
workedExamples.formula: Reliance on plant medicine increases with local availability, low price, community acceptance and scarcity of health services.
workedExamples.substitution: Village plants are locally available and low priced; the community accepts them; the nearest health care is distant and costly.
workedExamples.calculation: All four conditions favor plant medicine, so it becomes an important part of the local health care system.
workedExamples.answer: The village relies on plant medicine because it is locally available, affordable, accepted by the community and clinics are scarce.

workedExamples.problem: Property developers want to farm and settle on a slope that the Teso would treat as a sacred protected site. Use the Teso practice to predict the two different outcomes.
workedExamples.given: Option A permits farming, grazing and settlement; option B keeps the prohibition on human activity.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: human activity is prohibited in protected areas so that vegetation regenerates naturally.
workedExamples.substitution: Option A destroys the vegetation and drives away the species; option B keeps the site undisturbed.
workedExamples.calculation: Following the Teso record, undisturbed sites became very thick forests harboring many organisms.
workedExamples.answer: Option A leads to vegetation loss and habitat destruction; option B preserves the dense forest habitat for flora and fauna.

commonMistakes: Assuming indigenous knowledge is written in books; it was orally transferred across many generations.
Dismissing beliefs about spirits and sacred sites as having no conservation value, when they produced strictly protected, bio-rich forests.
Thinking conservation means banning all use of resources; the Teso still used wells and rivers for water and fish under rules.
Believing only modern technology and laws can conserve nature; indigenous rules protected sites for many generations.
Forgetting that reptiles like snakes, frogs and toads were deliberately protected as sustainers of water points.
Saying the reliance on plant medicine is due to culture alone, ignoring low prices, local availability and few health centers.
Treating indigenous knowledge as a recent invention; it has been the basis of conservation since ancient times.
applications: Ask elders in your community which places, trees or springs local rules protect, and record the reasons before the knowledge is lost.
Compare the Teso sacred sites with a locally respected protected area near your home and discuss how belief can support conservation.
Explain to a neighbor why protecting snakes and frogs at a water point, as the Teso did, can keep the water source healthy.
Use the four conditions of reliance on plant medicine to judge when a rural clinic should complement, not replace, plant remedies.
Relate the plant-medicine case to a nearby pharmacy market: cheap, locally accepted remedies travel far when clinics are few.
Write the review-essay of this unit about one exemplary indigenous conservation practice used by a community in your own area.
g10-geography-ug6-t3.summary: African communities hold enormous indigenous knowledge about biodiversity, accumulated over generations and transferred orally, which has been the basis of natural resource conservation on the continent. The Teso community of Busia County, Kenya, protected sacred burial sites from all human activity, allowing dense biodiverse forests to grow, and guarded rivers, wells and their reptiles with strong rules and beliefs. This knowledge remains valuable for managing environmental degradation and for the sustainable use of natural resources.

config.title: How the Teso Community Protected a Sacred Site

steps.label: Respect the spirits
steps.detail: Family spirits of long-buried relatives are believed to haunt the living.

steps.label: Perform Ekutet
steps.detail: Elderly men and women exhume remains at least ten years old, away from children and foreigners.

steps.label: Transfer and store
steps.detail: Special baskets carry the remains to a strictly protected central site.

steps.label: Ban activity
steps.detail: No farming, grazing or settlement is carried out there, since spirits attack disturbers.

steps.label: Nature regenerates
steps.detail: Vegetation grows into dense forests that harbor many species of flora and fauna.

pairs.q: How was indigenous knowledge transferred across generations?
pairs.a: Orally, among indigenous peoples of Africa, across many generations.

pairs.q: Give the four reasons for heavy reliance on plant medicine in Africa.
pairs.a: Local availability, low price, acceptance by local communities, and few health centers and medical professionals.

pairs.q: Which ceremony did the Teso use to recover the remains of the dead?
pairs.a: The Ekutet or Epunyas ceremony, performed by elderly men and women.

pairs.q: Why were snakes, frogs and toads protected at water points?
pairs.a: It was believed they helped maintain and sustain the lives of these important water points.

questions.q: Indigenous knowledge in Africa is mainly characterized by:
options: accumulation among indigenous peoples and oral transfer across generations
importation from Europe during colonization
recent invention by African governments
transfer through formal schools and universities
questions.explanation: Indigenous knowledge has been accumulated among indigenous peoples and orally transferred across many generations.

questions.q: Plant medicine became an important part of the health care system in Africa partly because health care centers and medical professionals are few, especially in rural areas.
questions.explanation: The textbook lists local availability, low price, community acceptance and the low number of health facilities as the reasons.

questions.q: In which county of Kenya did the case study of the Teso community take place?
questions.explanation: The case study was conducted in the Teso community in Busia County, Kenya.

questions.q: Which activities were prohibited in the Teso protected areas?
options: Farming, grazing of animals and settlement
Only hunting of large mammals
Drawing water from wells
Collecting fallen fruits
questions.explanation: Farming, grazing of animals and even settlements were prohibited in the protected areas.

questions.q: Explain how a strict prohibition on disturbing a sacred site led to a conservation outcome.
questions.answer: no human activity allowed vegetation to regenerate into dense forests|forests formed habitats for flora and fauna
questions.explanation: With no human activity, the sites remained very thick forests and became important habitats for a variety of flora and fauna.

questions.q: The Ekutet ceremony was carried out in the presence of children and foreigners.
questions.explanation: The ceremony was done in the absence of children and foreigners, by a special group of elderly men and women.

questions.q: How old, at a minimum, were the graves from which the Teso exhumed the remains of the dead?
questions.answer: ten years|at least ten years old
questions.explanation: Remains were dug out from graves that were at least ten years old.

questions.q: Why were reptiles such as snakes, frogs and toads protected by the Teso community?
options: Because of the belief that they helped sustain the important water points
Because they were valuable food for livestock
Because they were exported to other countries
Because the government fined anyone who harmed them
questions.explanation: The Teso protected these reptiles due to the belief that they helped maintain and sustain the lives of the ponds, rivers and wells.

questions.q: Give four uses for which African people highly depend on biological resources.
questions.explanation: Besides the well-known uses for food and building houses, Africans depend highly on biological resources for medicinal purposes.

questions.q: According to the unit summary, what is the key to survival in human-environment interactions?
options: Exploiting resources as fast as possible
Maintaining a suitable balance in interacting with the environment
Stopping all use of natural resources
Moving all people to cities
questions.explanation: Although interactions are inevitable for co-existence, maintaining a suitable balance is the key to survival.

questions.q: Arrange the Teso sacred-site protection chain correctly.
options: Dense forest forms habitat for flora and fauna
Remains exhumed and transferred by basket
All human activity banned in the site
Remains stored in a strictly protected central site
questions.explanation: The order is: exhume and transfer by basket, store in the protected site, ban human activity, then the dense forest forms.
